items.title: Debenhams returns to profit: Is the embattled department store finally turning a corner?
items.summary: We look at what caused the downfall of this titan of the high street, and whether its transformation efforts are paying off.
items.body:
Debenhams returns to profit: Is the embattled department store finally turning a corner?
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
Once a retail titan, Debenhams has had a difficult few years.
Fast-fashion firm Boohoo bought the department store chain out of administration in 2021, dispensing with its shops and going online-only in a major blow to the high street.
Debenhams has also been the subject of a long-running spat with retail veteran Mike Ashley, whose Frasers Group is its biggest shareholder.
More recently, Debenhams sold off youth brand Nasty Gal and announced the sudden departure of its chairman.
But it is not all bad. The retailer has long trailed a turnaround in its fortunes, and last week revealed its earnings had bounced back into profit in the previous six-month period.
Debenhams, which also owns the Karen Millen and Pretty Little Thing brands, cheered stronger sales and anticipates earnings to improve as it cuts costs.
Boss Dan Finley said: 'Our turnaround continues at pace. This is a strong first half, and, importantly, one where growth accelerated as we went through it.'
What caused Debenhams' downfall, and will its transformation efforts pay off?
Collapse: Debenhams went into administration in April 2020 and Boohoo Group, now known as Debenhams Group, purchased its brand and website
From high street giant to online challenger
Debenhams was once one of the best-known department store chains, but struggled with lower profits, rising debts and shoppers switching to online.
Its collapse in April 2020 led to the closure of all 124 of its shops and 12,000 job losses. Two hundred years of retail history disappeared in the blink of an eye.
Boohoo Group, founded in 2006 by Mahmud Kamani and Carol Kane, bought the Debenhams brand and website for £55million in 2021.
Following the acquisition, Boohoo Group rebranded itself in March 2025 to become Debenhams Group, operating across five core brands: Debenhams, Karen Millen, boohoo, BoohooMAN, Pretty Little Thing as well as several other labels such as Oasis and Warehouse.
Dan Finley: The current boss took up the role in 2024 and quickly launched a turnaround plan
Suddenly, Debenhams Group had to take the old-style Debenhams people knew and loved and turn it into a modern online retail brand without any physical shops.
Dan Finley joined Debenhams Group as chief executive of Debenhams in January 2022. He became the boss of the wider group two years later.
In a BBC podcast this year, Finley admitted he was unsure about taking on such a challenging role.
What went wrong for Debenhams?
The years that have followed the Boohoo group's acquisition of the Debenhams brand and website have been torrid.
Debenhams Group and other online retailers enjoyed a surge in demand during the pandemic, when many households went online to buy comfortable clothing to work and rest at home while high streets were closed.
But once shops reopened, retailers saw fresh competition from cheap Chinese sellers like Shein and Temu, as well as secondhand marketplaces such as Vinted and Depop. Online firms like Debenhams Group, and particularly its 'youth' brands, took a hit.
On a single day in July 2020, more than £1billion was wiped off the value of Debenhams Group, then still known as Boohoo Group, after it was revealed workers were paid less than the minimum wage at its Leicester garment factory.
In November 2024, Debenhams Group launched an investor cash call and raised just shy of £40million. Losses across Debenhams Group were widening and a spat with Frasers Group's boss, billionaire Mike Ashley ramped up.
In 2024, interim results showed Debenhams Group's losses had more than quadrupled. The group cut more than 1,000 jobs in the year to the end of February 2024 as its net debt rose to £95million.
It was also urging investors to reject Ashley's attempt to install himself as chief executive of Debenhams Group at an emergency meeting.
Billionaire Ashley, a shareholder in Debenhams Group, had wanted to acquire Debenhams physical shops but missed out on a deal.
By March 2025, Finley said sales for the group's founding brand, Boohoo, as well as BoohooMAN and Pretty Little Thing, had fallen sharply as 'we lost our way'.
Later that year, pre-tax losses widened to £263.9million, from £164.4million a year earlier, as revenue fell 12 per cent.
A tarnished reputation, dwindling sales, more competition and a growing debt pile left the group in need of a radical transformation.
Change is under way
That has seen Debenhams Group pivot to a marketplace-led business model that it says is 'capital-lite, stock-lite, cost-lite and cash generative'.
A marketplace model is when a retailer's website acts as a shop window, allowing third-party brands to sell items on its platform for a fee instead of stocking them itself.
Debenhams wants marketplace activity to account for well over half of gross merchandise value (GMV). This is the total value of goods sold before fees and returns.
When Finley became the group chief executive in November 2024, he began a multi-year transformation plan but warned it would take time, prompting nervousness among investors.
Debenhams Group has automated parts of its supply chain, and cut investment in brands like Warehouse, Oasis, Wallis and Dorothy Perkins.
This month, it sold its Sheffield distribution centre for £90million, with the lease reassigned to Primark. It also sold youth brand Nasty Gal to New York-based White Space, which also owns Von Dutch, for nearly £12million.
Row: Debenhams Group has been embroiled in various spats with shareholder Mike Ashley
Jonathan De Mello, founder of retail consultants JDM Retail, told This is Money: 'The group initially floundered because it was weighed down by an asset-heavy infrastructure, soaring logistics costs, and massive customer return rates just as the post-pandemic online shopping boom collapsed.
'Unwinding a legacy fast-fashion empire is taking a long time because transitioning millions of customers and thousands of suppliers onto an entirely new tech and operational ecosystem requires a total structural overhaul.'
Has the group reached a turning point?
The sale of the group's Sheffield distribution centre is significant and should leave Debenhams Group's net debt at a negligible level by February 2027.
Debt has been a key sticking point for investors, so the offloading of lease costs will go some way in strengthening its bottom line.
In June 2026, the group said annual losses before tax fell to £108.6million in the year ending February 28, an improvement on the previous year.
In its most recent update, Debenhams Group said it expected earnings to continue to improve amid further cost cuts.
Adjusted earnings jumped 13.9 per cent to £24million, driven by the Debenhams brand, which accounted for 41 per cent of GMV.
The firm said it was on track to secure £100million in cost savings by next year.
On September 18, Debenhams Group announced its chairman, Tim Morris, was leaving the business with immediate effect, replaced by Iain McDonald.
McDonald, who is a significant shareholder in Debenhams Group, was previously on the firm's board from June 2017 to February 2026.
Debenhams Group said the reappointment came as its 'focus moves to rebuilding equity value' in the business after making progress in its turnaround efforts.
Mike Ashley's Frasers Group previously wrote to Morris threatening to hold a shareholder vote over his position at the business.
Jonathan De Mello added: 'While the results show the turnaround strategy entails a necessary pivot toward a lower-risk, asset-light digital marketplace model - evidenced by the offloading of the Sheffield automation hub and the Nasty Gal brand - it is premature to say the group has turned a corner.
'Fragile consumer confidence and intense competition from aggressive, ultra-cheap global players like Shein and Temu continue to heavily impact the business, meaning that while Q2 volume ticked up slightly to 2.9 per cent, Debenhams Group is still very much in financial triage mode as it attempts to permanently stabilise its baseline.'
Are Debenhams shares a buy?
Last autumn, shares in Aim-listed Debenhams Group plummeted to as low as 11.3p, but they have since recovered to around 25p.
The latest trading update offers some relief to investors, as Debenhams Group continues to cut its debt and boost earnings.
Russ Mould, investment director at AJ Bell, added: 'Several key brands returned to growth and the core Debenhams brand is also performing robustly despite a backdrop which is about as gloomy as a wet day in late November.'
He added: 'Critically the company has made real progress with its balance sheet, partly thanks to disposals and as it focuses more heavily on cash generation. This will inspire greater confidence in the group's ability to see its way through what looks set to be a testing period.'
Others think the retail group could still run into issues.
Lale Akoner, an analyst at eToro, said: 'We still think that the shares remain a high-risk turnaround bet. Investors accepting volatility may see value, but sustained sales growth and positive free cash flow would provide proof.'

items.body:
Superdrug has officially relaunched its refurbished store at Merry Hill, owned and operated by Redical, following a major transformation, making it the largest store in the retailer’s UK estate. The relaunch marks the latest milestone in Superdrug’s ongoing investment in its bricks-and-mortar portfolio.
Now spanning 12,831 sq. ft., the transformed store will create 15 new permanent roles, alongside 10 seasonal positions over the Christmas period. The investment forms part of Superdrug’s wider expansion plans, which will see the retailer open 30 new stores across the UK this year,
To celebrate the reopening, customers visiting on opening day can enjoy a live DJ set, while the first 50 shoppers through the doors will receive a £10 Superdrug voucher.
Inside, customers will find an even wider range of international and trending beauty brands, including Biodance and Medicube, alongside much-loved Superdrug own-brand favourites such as Studio London, B. Skin, Me+, Vitamin E and Optimum. The refurbished store also features an extensive premium fragrance collection, bringing some of the latest and most popular scents together under one roof, as well as a pharmacy, aesthetics clinic and piercing studio.
Superdrug is also continuing the expansion of its accredited Aesthetics Clinic offering with the reopening of the refreshed store, registered with CQC (Care Quality Commission), marking another milestone in the retailer’s commitment to delivering safe, accessible and regulated aesthetic treatments on the high street.
Customers can also make the most of their visits by signing up to Superdrug’s Health & Beautycard and VIP Rewards programmes. Members can earn points on purchases and redeem them at a later date, as well as accessing exclusive benefits including lower prices, bonus point promotions, birthday treats and the option to pay with points.
Superdrug Property Director, Clare Jennings said: “We’re delighted to be opening the doors to our newly refurbished store at Merry Hill, which is now the largest store in our estate. The 12,831 sq. ft. store brings together everything customers love about Superdrug, from great value across health, beauty and wellbeing to the latest international beauty trends and much-loved own-brand favourites.”
“Our refurbished store gives customers the chance to explore our dedicated Beauty Studio, discover an extensive premium fragrance collection and shop the latest trends across beauty and skincare. We’re excited to welcome both new and existing Superdrug customers and hope they enjoy discovering everything our refurbished store has to offer”
Alistair Winning, Leasing Manager for Redical, said: “The full reopening of Superdrug in its new, significantly expanded format marks an important milestone for Merry Hill, reinforcing our position as a leading destination for health, beauty and wellness. As Merry Hill continues to evolve, the unveiling of the UK’s largest Superdrug store demonstrates our commitment to delivering an increasingly compelling offer for visitors, and the growing appeal of the destination for best-in-class retailers.”

items.body:
British Land has announced that popular national coffee shop Black Sheep Coffee will open two new stores at Glasgow Fort and Fort Kinnaird, strengthening the food and beverage offering across its leading Scottish retail destinations.
The coffee brand will occupy a 2,500sq ft unit at Glasgow Fort and a 2,000sq ft unit at Fort Kinnaird, adding further choice for visitors and complementing the existing retail, leisure and dining offer at both locations.
The openings reflect British Land’s ongoing focus on broadening the mix of uses across its retail destinations, bringing in high-quality food and beverage operators that complement the existing retail and leisure offer. By expanding the range of places to eat, drink and meet, British Land is continuing to evolve both destinations in line with changing visitor expectations.
It also builds on wider leasing momentum across British Land’s Scottish portfolio. Fast-growing chicken shop Wingstop UKI opened restaurants at both retail parks this summer, as part of a wider seven-site agreement with British Land, further expanding the range of food and beverage operators available at both destinations.
The openings add to a period of continued investment across British Land’s Scottish portfolio. In May, British Land submitted plans for a 60,000sq ft retail and leisure expansion at Glasgow Fort, including an extension of more than 32,000sq ft to the existing Marks & Spencer store and a new leisure offer featuring bowling, arcades and other attractions.
This was followed in June by plans for more than 42,500sq ft of new retail and leisure space at Fort Kinnaird, including a new food store and an enhanced leisure offer designed to complement the destination’s existing leisure quarter.
Ross McCall, retail leasing and commercialisation director at British Land, said: “Welcoming two new national brands to both Fort Kinnaird and Glasgow Fort is a huge sign of confidence in the resilience of the retail parks that we have created in Scotland. We are always looking to develop and grow the offering for our visitors, giving them reasons to keep coming back, and creating a compelling retail and leisure mix that blends national and independent brands helps us achieve that.
“The openings build on our recent investment announcements, that will ensure that both Glasgow Fort and Fort Kinnaird keep delivering new and exciting experiences for our customers now and in the future.”

items.body:
At first sight The Middle Ale in Dundonald, Northern Ireland looks just like any other pub. There is a big TV, an array of seating, and beer pumps behind the bar. Look a little closer, however, and you might ask why there are packets of fajitas and gravy granules on the walls.
That’s because the pub belongs to the supermarket chain Lidl, but the Middle Ale (like “middle aisle”, get it?) isn’t just a wacky marketing stunt. Northern Ireland has ultra-strict laws around licences to sell alcohol, whether as a shop, pub or nightclub. Lidl tried to get a licence to sell alcohol in its Dundonald store, and was refused, but after a court battle it did manage to get a licence for a pub – which it duly opened next door, selling alcohol to take away as well as serving drinks in the pub itself.
It’s an absurd chapter of a much bigger story: local activists have long demanded licensing reform that could invigorate Northern Irish nightlife.
The Lidl pub situation exposed “the hypocrisy of everything we’re up against,” says Boyd Sleator. In 2021, Sleator and Belfast-based DJ Holly Lester co-founded Free the Night, a charitable organisation formed in 2021 with the aim of creating a safe and progressive nightlife in Northern Ireland.
Research conducted by Free the Night claims that obtaining an alcohol licence in Northern Ireland costs, on average, £75,250, but they say they have heard of sums up to £1m changing hands. This is because the current “surrender principle” means that any new pub or club must buy an existing licence from another establishment, a unique “one-in, one out” law. It must also prove an inadequacy of licensed premises to serve the local community.
According to the BBC, The Middle Ale cost Lidl more than £500,000 and took six years of planning, numbers that Sleator and Lester say expose the barriers facing those keen to open new venues in the country. “[That’s] something no local can do,” claims Sleator. “In a way I’m glad they did it because it helps us expose how shit the current system is.”
There is no suggestion of wrongdoing by Lidl. The company did not respond to multiple requests for comment. Gordon Cruikshanks, managing director for Lidl Northern Ireland, previously told the BBC that the pub “was the best option to be able to provide the community in Dundonald with our full range of products”, but any changes to licensing laws were “for others to continue to discuss”.
Free the Night is mounting a legal challenge over the minister for communities’ decision to reject a 2025 independent review of liquor licensing conducted by the University of Stirling. Key among Free the Night’s aims is a comprehensive review of alcohol licensing legislation, including the removal of the surrender principle. Northern Irish musicians including Bicep, David Holmes and Max Cooper signed an open letter outlining their demands.
In a statement, the Department for Communities told the Guardian: “As legal proceedings are ongoing; it would be inappropriate for the Department to comment.”
Lester began work on Free the Night during the pandemic when she lost her DJ gigs and returned home to Belfast. “I was shocked at how things were regressing,” she says. “The nightlife ecosystem seemed to be in a worse position than when I’d left eight years previously.”
Lester says she finds the night-time economy in Northern Ireland to be “incredibly restrictive” because there are “basically no venues here”. Strict closing times are also problematic, meaning promoters are “trying to cram everything into this very small time frame”. The knock-on effects mean that promoters are less able to attract international talent while also struggling to give opportunities to local talent.
Both point to Ulster Sports Club, a historic venue that closed in 2018 before reopening under new management a year later, as an example of one thriving Belfast venue. Bands including English Teacher and Mary in the Junkyard have played there while its 3am weekend closing time offers an opportunity for late-night partying.
Sleator has a background in human-rights advocacy, including work around abortion rights and same-sex marriage. He is used to butting heads with the local authorities and speaks of a culture that cares more about the past than the future. “We’ve got an incredibly divided government who still only care about green and orange [traditional Nationalist and Unionist] issues,” he says. The pair also can’t help feeling that their dream of 24-hour clubbing is a little too utopian for those in government. “There’s an attitude of ‘You shouldn’t be shaking your hips, that’s the devil’s work’,” Sleator says with a grim chuckle.
One key aim of Free the Night is to give musicians the spaces they need to thrive. The current lack of these has created a “creative drain”, they say. Their research shows that 70% of creatives had thought about leaving Northern Ireland, with 60% actually making the move.
DJ Or:la, who signed Free the Night’s open letter, says she has “harboured a real frustration with the licensing laws and lack of venues across the country” since she was a teenager. She has felt “pushed out” in her bid to pursue a career in music and now lives in Liverpool.
“It’s clear that Belfast and Northern Ireland more broadly are not yet seen as nightlife destinations in the way that cities such as Berlin, Amsterdam and others across the UK are,” she says. She adds that while Northern Ireland is “flourishing in many areas” its nightlife “seems to be moving backwards”.
A court date originally scheduled for mid-September has been delayed as Free the Night requires extra funds to continue its legal action. Free the Night believes that the authorities are overlooking the opportunities that a thriving nightlife economy could bring.
“We see clubs and live music venues as spaces that can break down prejudices,” Sleator says. He cites his time raving in the 90s as proof of how music can bring people together. “There’s a lot of stuff in Northern Ireland which is like, ‘Let’s get Catholics and Protestants into a room together …’ We were just going there organically. I think that that’s where a lot of peace-building happened.”

Welfare-led challenger grows from 43 launch stores to 130 unique Asda stores, reshaping its range around proven 10-pack demand. items.body:
Welfare-led challenger grows from 43 launch stores to 130 unique Asda stores, reshaping its range around proven 10-pack demand.
Better Eggs is set to more than triple its Asda footprint from 43 launch stores to 130 unique stores from Week 38, almost exactly one year after the brand first arrived on shelf.
The expansion follows a first year in which the latest Asda sales-by-SKU export records £631,974.53 in retail sales across 264,896 packs in the 50 complete weeks from 15 September 2025 to 24 August 2026. That equates to 2,103,596 individual eggs sold before the brand had reached its first anniversary.
From Week 38, Better Eggs 6 Large and the new Better Eggs 10 Large will each be listed in 125 Asda stores, in an identical store estate. Better Eggs 10 Mixed Weight will be available in 70 stores, while 6 Medium will leave the range.
The existing 10 Mixed Weight pack has been the biggest value driver in year one, generating £354,760.46 and accounting for 56.1% of Better Eggs sales value. Its 128,555 packs represented 1,285,550 individual eggs, or 61.1% of the brand’s egg volume in the period. The performance helped inform the decision to add a second 10-pack format for year two.
Better Eggs was created in Lincolnshire to bring clearer differentiation to the egg fixture. Its free-range hens are kept at 8.1 birds per square metre, 10% below the standard free-range maximum of 9.0, giving them more space to live and roam.
The brand also grows grain in Lincolnshire, mills feed through its own system and operates a fully traceable supply chain centred within approximately 25 miles. Better Eggs is RSPCA Assured and covered by the British Lion Code.
The first year has also brought industry recognition. Better Eggs was named The Grocer’s Top Launch 2025 in eggs, became a Startup of the Year finalist at The Grocer Gold Awards 2026, received a 1-Star Great Taste Award 2026, and is shortlisted in the Home Baking category of the Great British Food Awards 2026.
“A year ago Better Eggs was a new brand in 43 Asda stores. In the latest complete sales data, shoppers have bought 2,103,596 eggs and now we are moving into 130 stores. For me, that is the proof that there is room in the category for something genuinely different. We did not build Better Eggs just to put another green box on the fixture. We built it from the hen upwards and then watched what shoppers actually did. The biggest lesson from year one is to follow the data. The 10 Mixed pack became our strongest value driver, so we have reshaped the range around what people are buying and introduced 10 Large for year two. We are proud of the first year, but this is really the starting point,” said Henry O’Connor, creator of Better Eggs.
“Better Eggs combines the farming infrastructure and experience of a long-established British egg producer with the pace and ambition of a challenger brand. The first year has given us confidence to keep investing behind the next stage of growth while protecting the welfare, quality and supply standards behind the proposition,” said Daniel Fairburn, chief executive, L.J. Fairburn & Son.
The Week 38 expansion lands in the same week as Better Eggs’ first anniversary and marks the brand’s largest distribution step since launch.

items.title: Asda audio campaign delivers more than 20x return on ad spend through Experian and Bauer measurement

Experian and Bauer Media have demonstrated the commercial impact of audio advertising for Asda, with new campaign measurement revealing a more than 20x return on advertising spend (ROAS), 13% higher transactional spend and 27.5% higher customer retention among exposed audiences compared with a control group. Working with Asda’s media agency, Spark Foundry, Experian and Bauer […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Experian and Bauer Media have demonstrated the commercial impact of audio advertising for Asda, with new campaign measurement revealing a more than 20x return on advertising spend (ROAS), 13% higher transactional spend and 27.5% higher customer retention among exposed audiences compared with a control group.
Working with Asda’s media agency, Spark Foundry, Experian and Bauer Media connected exposure to an Asda campaign running across Bauer Media’s audioXi network with real-world transactional spend data. The analysis enabled Spark Foundry and Asda to move beyond traditional media metrics such as reach, impressions and engagement to understand whether the campaign translated into measurable commercial outcomes.
The measurement also identified which audience groups delivered the strongest commercial returns, providing insight that can be used to inform future audience targeting and media investment.
The analysis used Experian’s privacy-first identity capabilities to connect devices exposed to the campaign to households and match these with Experian’s Transactional Spend Data. Drawing on purchase behaviour across more than 3,500 brands from one in ten UK credit and debit account holders and modelled to represent the wider UK population, the data provides a privacy-safe view of consumer spending without revealing personal or sensitive consumer data.
Experian then combined transactional spend data with its Mosaic consumer segmentation to identify the demographic, lifestyle and behavioural 
Debbie Oates, director of customer engagement, Experian Marketing Services UK&I, said: “Advertisers are under growing pressure to demonstrate what their media investment is delivering for the business. Reach and engagement remain important measures, but marketers increasingly need to understand whether exposure translates into changes in real customer behaviour.
“By connecting media exposure with transactional spend and customer intelligence, we can help advertisers understand both the commercial impact of a campaign and the audiences driving those results. For Spark Foundry, this means being able to demonstrate to their client, Asda, not only that audio is effectively reaching and engaging customers, but exactly how that investment contributes to spend, retention and return on investment, and using those findings to make future campaigns even more effective.”
Rosie Dawson, group account director, Spark Foundry, said: “Our first trial of using the audioXi and Experian partnership was a huge success. The granularity of data has been invaluable to understand our target audiences and enhance our use of audioXi moving forwards.”
Charlie Brookes, director of digital, Bauer Media, added: “audioXi gives advertisers access to the scale and diversity of the UK’s digital audio audience, reaching more than 14 million listeners every week. That combination of scale, quality inventory and sophisticated targeting makes audioXi a powerful proposition for brands looking to engage audiences at scale – and, as this Asda campaign demonstrates, to connect that engagement to tangible commercial outcomes.
“By combining our audience reach with Experian’s transactional data, we can help advertisers move beyond impressions and demonstrate the real business value their audio investment is delivering.”
Experian and Bauer Media’s measurement partnership enables advertisers to connect campaign exposure with real-world spending behaviour and customer intelligence. By bringing together identity, transactional data and consumer insight, the partnership helps advertisers understand what their campaigns are delivering commercially and apply those learnings to future media planning.

items.body:
The Perfume Shop, the UK’s largest specialist perfume retailer, has launched its 2026 Christmas recruitment programme, with around 800 temporary Christmas Sales Assistant roles becoming available across the UK and Ireland ahead of the festive season.
Vacancies have already opened in selected locations, with hundreds more set to go live throughout September and early October. Nearly every The Perfume Shop store will welcome at least one temporary Christmas Sales Assistant this year, as the retailer strengthens its teams ahead of one of the busiest periods in the retail calendar.
Alongside supporting stores during the Christmas rush, this year’s recruitment programme will provide hundreds of people with the chance to build hands-on workplace experience. The Perfume Shop is particularly encouraging applications from young people entering employment for the first time, for whom a seasonal position can provide an accessible first step into the world of work.
Working on the shop floor during the fast-paced festive period gives new starters experience that extends well beyond retail, from learning how to communicate with different customers and work effectively as part of a team, to problem solving and building confidence in a professional environment.
Christmas Sales Assistants will be supported with training to prepare them for the festive season and will work alongside The Perfume Shop’s experienced Perfume People, helping customers find the perfect fragrance for one of the biggest gifting occasions of the year.
Seasonal perfume people have the opportunity to earn commission in addition to their hourly pay and receive an employee discount on products. Wellbeing support is available through the Retail Trust and Stream, providing resources to support people’s mental, physical and financial wellbeing. While these roles provide an opportunity for those taking their first steps into employment, applications are open to people at all stages of their working lives, whether looking for additional income over Christmas, wanting to build experience or simply seeking a new challenge during the festive period.
Michelle Fellows, people, sustainability & development director at The Perfume Shop, says: “Our Christmas perfume people become an important part of our store teams at the busiest and most exciting time of the year. With around 800 opportunities becoming available across the UK and Ireland, we’re looking forward to welcoming lots of new faces into the business.
A seasonal role can be a great way to experience the workplace for the first time and learn what it’s like to be part of a busy team. You’re interacting with customers, learning from experienced people you work with and developing confidence every day, all while helping people find something special for Christmas. We want everyone who joins us for the festive season to get something valuable from their time at The Perfume Shop, whether that’s new skills, greater confidence, additional income or experience that helps them decide where they want to go next.”
Recruitment is now underway, with further Christmas Sales Assistant vacancies set to be released throughout September and early October.

items.title: Ordered online, picked in-store: why quick commerce depends on robust store processes

Fast delivery does not start on the last mile. In quick commerce, the process inside the store already decides whether an online order is ready on time, complete and accurate. At NRF Retail’s Big Show Europe 2026, Continente demonstrated how closely e-commerce and store operations are now intertwined. The Portuguese grocery retailer runs its quick […] If you want more information Retail Times get in touch! Retail Times - Retail Times, a free to view retail news website
items.body:
Fast delivery does not start on the last mile. In quick commerce, the process inside the store already decides whether an online order is ready on time, complete and accurate.
At NRF Retail’s Big Show Europe 2026, Continente demonstrated how closely e-commerce and store operations are now intertwined. The Portuguese grocery retailer runs its quick commerce fulfilment entirely with store staff. Across Europe, pure dark store models have come under considerable economic pressure. That makes this store-based approach particularly relevant for retailers with an existing branch network.
Why quick commerce can fail before the order leaves the store
Continente has been operating online grocery since 2001. As Guilherme Cardoso, head of e-commerce at Sonae MC, explained, customer expectations have shifted. Shoppers no longer want to choose between speed and quality; they expect both. The internal complexity behind the service should remain invisible to them.
That complexity sits in the store. The workflow runs from the online order to the store order, through picking and stock updates, to staging and handover. If any step breaks down, even the best delivery promise is worthless.
The typical failure points are well known. Items are not at their expected shelf location, the system shows stock that is not physically there, or paper pick lists lead to long search times and queries. On top of this, store staff handle customers, shelf replenishment and online orders at the same time.
How stores can pick online orders quickly and accurately
According to Continente, the retailer used data to rethink its picking process. This is the right approach, because speed in store fulfilment comes primarily from removing friction. That means clear order allocation, short walking routes through the store and scan confirmation for every item picked.
In grocery, checking best-before dates and maintaining the cold chain are also part of the job. If an item is missing, a decision is needed immediately: a substitute, where the customer has accepted substitutions, or a short pick. This information has to flow straight back into stock. Otherwise the online shop will sell the same unavailable item again with the next order.
What inaccurate stock data costs in store fulfilment
Every short pick creates follow-up costs: rework, customer queries, refunds and, in the worst case, cancelled orders. The loss of trust is just as serious. Customers who repeatedly receive incomplete grocery orders will take their next basket elsewhere.
At the same time, inefficient picking ties up staff who are then missing from the shop floor. For retailers running quick commerce from their existing store network, process quality is therefore a matter of profitability.
How store fulfilment processes can be managed digitally
COSYS digitalises operational retail processes between stores, warehouse and head office. Its modular platform covers in-store picking, inventory management, best-before date checks and task management in a single mobile app. Using the COSYS WebDesk, head office manages orders and keeps track of processing status in every store. Integrations with ERP and merchandise management systems ensure that stock changes do not have to be re-entered manually.
The overall system includes suitable mobile computers from Zebra, Honeywell and Datalogic, mobile printers for order labels and smart lockers as pickup points for click-and-collect orders. MDE services and COSYS MDM keep the device fleet operational across all locations.
Process data and AI as a basis for decisions
Process data analysis shows where time is lost in store fulfilment. In addition, COSYS AI answers questions based on the data captured in the WebDesk. Examples include “Which stores had the most short picks on online orders last month?”, “For which items does booked stock most often differ from the picking result?” and “At what times of day does picking take longest?”
Retailers do not need to start with a complete solution. They can begin with picking or inventory management, for example, and then expand step by step with additional modules, devices and stores. This limits both investment risk and implementation effort.
Practical tip: measure search time before you shorten the delivery promise
Before discussing faster delivery times, take an honest look at the shop floor. Shadow a picker for a full shift and note every item that cannot be found at the first attempt. This list often reveals more precisely than any KPI where stock data, shelf placement and processes have drifted apart. That is exactly where quick commerce can genuinely become faster.
Looking to run quick commerce and store fulfilment reliably from your stores?
Contact the COSYS team for individual advice on picking, inventory management, best-before date checks, task management and process data analysis. Book an appointment at vertrieb@cosys.de or +49 5062 900 0.
Alternatively, try the free COSYS Retail demo app for Android and iOS.

items.body:
Asda and InPost, the UK’s leading out-of-home parcel locker provider, have today announced a major new partnership that will see up to 700 InPost Lockers installed across Asda’s UK store estate.
The partnership will give millions of Asda customers a convenient new way to send, collect and return parcels while they shop, and marks one of InPost’s most significant UK retail partnerships to date.
The rollout forms part of Asda’s continued investment in services that make life easier for customers and enhance the convenience of shopping in-store.
The easy-to-use parcel lockers will be installed across a mix of Asda superstores, supermarkets and Express locations, enabling customers to collect, send and return parcels at a time that suits them.
The launch builds on the growing demand for out-of-home delivery solutions, as consumers increasingly look for greater flexibility and control over when and where they send and receive parcels.
As part of InPost’s growing UK network of more than 16,000 lockers, the partnership underlines the accelerating shift towards out-of-home delivery in the UK. The commitment to install up to 700 Lockers across Asda’s estate will significantly broaden access to InPost’s network and strengthen the role of lockers as a mainstream alternative to traditional home delivery.
Joseph Sutton, director – Express, Fuel & Wholesale, said: “Our unmatched mix of services is a key part of what sets Asda apart, and we know customers increasingly value the convenience of being able to tick off multiple tasks in a single trip.
“We’re delighted to be partnering with InPost to bring parcel lockers to up to 700 locations nationwide. This rollout gives customers a fast and flexible way to collect and return parcels, seamlessly fitting around their weekly shop and making everyday life a little easier.”
Paul Selvey, network director at InPost UK, commented: “This is a major milestone for InPost in the UK. Partnerships with household-name retailers like Asda are central to our ambition to make out-of-home delivery as easy and accessible as possible for consumers across the country.
“Asda’s scale and nationwide footprint give us a significant opportunity to bring InPost Lockers closer to millions more people. Partnerships like this are helping change the way people think about parcel delivery and making lockers an increasingly established part of the UK delivery landscape.”
You can find your nearest InPost Locker by visiting: InPost | InPost Lockers are coming to Asda stores

items.body:
As student Freshers’ Weeks begin across the country, Lidl GB has teamed up with renowned budget chef Miguel Barclay to create seven healthy student suppers for £7. With research showing that perceptions of cost are the biggest barrier to healthy eating, the quick and easy recipes demonstrate that eating well for both health and the planet can fit a student budget.
The new recipes are inspired by the principles of the Planetary Health Diet and the UK’s Eatwell Guide, encouraging students to adopt healthier and more sustainable food habits by making simple swaps such as incorporating a greater variety of plant-based foods and choosing wholegrain options.
For young people, the desire to eat healthily already exists, but the perception that it has to cost more can be prohibitive. In fact, 65% of 18-34 year olds say they actively try to eat healthily every day or most of the time, yet 57% have chosen less healthy options in the past year because they believed that was cheaper, according to research commissioned by Lidl.
To kick-start the new university year, Lidl is giving students the chance to win a “Live Well Golden Ticket” through Lidl Plus, giving them one free Live Well product each week for the rest of the year. Lidl’s Live Well marker helps shoppers identify products that support personal and planetary health.
For a chance to win one of 1,000 exclusive Golden Tickets, students can visit this link before midnight on 2nd October and enter their name, university or college name, email address and mobile number associated with their Lidl Plus account.
Georgina Hall, director of corporate affairs at Lidl GB, said: “Starting university or college is often the first time young people are responsible for cooking and shopping for themselves, making affordable, balanced meals that are simple to prepare especially important. We’re proud to be a student favourite for customers seeking quality and value, and we want to support them to make healthier, more sustainable choices throughout the academic year via our Live Well range, market-leading value, and Lidl Plus rewards.”
Miguel Barclay, chef and creator of the One Pound Meals series, said: “Student budgets can be tight, but that shouldn’t restrict access to delicious, healthy meals. I’ve really enjoyed reimagining some classic student staples with an approach that’s nutritious, kind to the planet and affordable. The seven meals for £7 elevate simple ingredients into delicious and filling meals via step-by-step recipes that will be easy to recreate in student halls – helping them to eat well without eating into their budget.”
Inspired by the principles of the Planetary Health Diet and The Eatwell Guide, Lidl GB’s seven affordable and achievable meals give this year’s freshers a practical introduction to healthier eating habits that they can carry with them throughout student life and beyond.
To try Miguel’s recipes, check out the website here.

items.title: Claire’s Accessories administrators hand creditors nearly £10m bill
items.summary: The administrators of collapsed jewellery retailer Claire’s Accessories have billed nearly £10m for their work, with bosses charging more than £1,500 per hour. The retail chain collapsed for the second time in January, just months after private equity firm Modella Capital bought it out of administration last September.  The double collapse of Claire’s looks set [...]
items.body:
Claire’s Accessories administrators hand creditors nearly £10m bill
The administrators of collapsed jewellery retailer Claire’s Accessories have billed nearly £10m for their work, with bosses charging more than £1,500 per hour.
The retail chain collapsed for the second time in January, just months after private equity firm Modella Capital bought it out of administration last September.
The double collapse of Claire’s looks set to hand two of the City’s top consultancy firms a blockbuster payday, as administrators bemoaned a “significantly higher volume of work” than expected.
Interpath, the administrators for the original collapse of Claire’s Accessories, had initially charged creditors about £4m for their work.
But following the retailer’s second collapse, Interpath said it had asked creditors to grant the consultancy an additional £3.2m for the extra work, bringing their total bill to more than £7.2m.
The consultancy said they had to continue trading the business for 15 weeks following its collapse, overseeing more than 2,000 employees across about 300 shops.
“As a result, a larger and more senior administration team was maintained for a longer period than originally anticipated,” Interpath said.
“Further time costs are also expected to be incurred as a result of the extension of the administration period, which has been necessary to manage the orderly run-off of the Company’s property portfolio.”
Bosses charge £1.5k per hour
Will Wright, Interpath’s UK chief executive, and Chris Pole, the head of its Midlands and South team, had been billing creditors an hourly rate of £1,410 for their work, but hiked this to £1,515 from April.
Across Interpath’s team, administrators charged an average rate of £909 per hour, totalling time costs of more than £1m.
Interpath’s bill comes on top of the costs incurred by the administrators of Cauki Ltd, the company set up by Modella to complete its purchase of Claire’s.
New York-headquartered consultancy Kroll has been overseeing this administration and has logged time costs of about £2.2m at an average rate of £510 per hour.
This could take the total costs of Claire’s Accessories’ administration to more than £7.4m, though the retailer’s creditors are yet to approve these pay deals.
Modella has snapped up a number of struggling retailers in recent years. Last year, it bought WH Smith’s 480 high street stores for £40m, before renaming them TG Jones.
The newly-named stores have faced difficult trading since their change of ownership. Modella recently pushed through a drastic restructuring which could force the closure of 150 sites.

items.title: Boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher sounds alarm over business rates raid on larger stores
items.summary: The boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher has sounded the alarm over the risk of a business rates raid on larger stores in next month's Budget.
items.body:
Boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher sounds alarm over business rates raid on larger stores
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
The boss of B&Q owner Kingfisher has sounded the alarm over the risk of a business rates raid on larger stores in next month’s Budget.
Thierry Garnier joined a chorus of retail chiefs in urging Labour not to hit big premises as part of reforms to the hated commercial property tax.
Garnier said: ‘Big stores are very often big anchors in retail parks and in high streets, large employers in cities. So we very much hope that the larger stores won’t be penalised in the coming weeks.’
The comments came as Kingfisher – which also owns Screwfix as well as European brands Castorama and Brico Depot – upgraded its full-year profit outlook after publishing strong first half results.
That was despite a setback for B&Q, which saw summer sales hit by the heatwave and weak demand for its bathroom range, which is now being revamped. Instead, customers preferred to splash out on their kitchens.
Garnier said: ‘People are spending more money on their kitchen today than on their bathroom… a more important part of our lives, it’s becoming a more important room in the house, and we see that across Europe – a more positive trend on kitchen than bathroom.’
B&Q has more than 300 stores
Shares rose 9pc in early trading as the UK-listed group said adjusted profits for the six months to 31 July rose 10pc to £404m, driven by higher margins and cost control.
It is now forecasting full-year profits of £595m-£635m, versus previous guidance of £565m-£625m.
However, like-for-like sales rose by just 0.3pc and Garnier admitted that ‘the consumer environment remains mixed’.
In the UK, Screwfix sales jumped 5.6pc in the first half but B&Q struggled, with a fall of 2.9pc. The brand saw a notable 8.1pc slump in demand for ‘big ticket’ items in the second quarter.
Screwfix has more than 981 stores in the UK and Ireland while B&Q has 318.
Garnier, who is quitting Kingfisher to become the boss of Netherlands-based supermarket group Ahold Delhaize shrugged off a question about his departure.
He said: ‘I’m fully committed and focused on Kingfisher. The board has a well-prepared succession plan. The search is ongoing and moving at pace.’
On the Budget, Garnier said: ‘We believe that retail is a powerful engine for growth, it is an engine of employment, and we hope the government can see it in the same way.
‘Stability and certainty is always what you look for as a business.
‘For us, the number one priority is business rates… in the longer term, we need a level playing field between bricks-and-mortar and online players.
‘When you are a brick and mortar retailer and when you are a pure online company you don’t pay the same tax and that will create more and more issues in the future.’
But his fears over the impact of larger stores echo those expressed by the bosses of other major retailers in recent weeks.
Sports Direct billionaire Mike Ashley has said the Government would be ‘simply delusional’ to heap more pressure on big retailers.
Some firms fear Prime Minister Andy Burnham and Chancellor John Healey are plotting a fresh business rates raid on large shops to fund lower bills for pubs and music venues.
They are particularly concerned that rates paid by large stores, which are deemed to have a rateable value of £500,000 or more, will be increased.
Outgoing John Lewis boss Peter Ruis said earlier this month that it would have ‘a terrible impact for all retailers’.

items.title: Post Office boss calls for tax breaks to save rural branches
items.summary: The boss of the Post Office has urged ministers to save village branches from crippling hikes in business rates.
items.body:
Post Office boss calls for tax breaks to save rural branches
- See more This is Money on Google - save us as a Preferred Source
The boss of the Post Office has urged ministers to save village branches from crippling hikes in business rates.
Chief executive Neil Brocklehurst said post offices play a ‘similarly vital role in communities’ to pubs, which have been handed support with the commercial property levy.
He said post offices also need ‘urgent help’ in the form of ‘targeted relief’.
Controversial changes in last year’s Budget mean post offices will pay nearly £45million in business rates this year – an increase of £29million.
Nearly 600 branches will have to pay rates for the first time.
Writing for the Daily Mail, Brocklehurst said: ‘There is a contradiction at the heart of the Government’s ambition for growth. We say we want thriving high streets and essential services within easy reach of every community. But many of the businesses delivering exactly that are facing a sharp increase in costs.’
Post offices will pay almost £45million in business rates this year - an increase of £29million
He added: ‘Government has already accepted that pubs merit financial support because of their wider social and economic contribution to communities – with a 20 per cent cut to their business rates bill set to come into effect in England next year. Few would dispute the important role pubs play in bringing people together. But post offices play a similarly vital role in communities.
‘If Government is serious about growth in every postcode, then it should recognise the unique role post offices play in making that growth possible. That is why postmasters are calling for targeted business rates relief.’
There were 11,708 post office branches in the UK as of February 2026, according to a recent report from the Office for National Statistics. It said that the number of branches has remained relatively stable since 2009.
The business is hoping to extend its network and opening hours by 2030.
Brocklehurst is just the latest businessman to call for reform of the rates system.
Writing for the Daily Mail on Monday, Mark Allan, the boss of commercial property giant Landsec, said a shake-up was required to help firms tackle Britain’s youth unemployment crisis.
He said the growing number of youngsters not in education, employment or training – so-called NEETs – was ‘a catastrophe in slow motion for our economy’.
‘It’s become increasingly clear that addressing the NEET crisis can’t be viewed solely through the narrow lens of skills and education,’ said Allan.
‘It should go without saying that businesses also need the capacity to create entry-level jobs, something that has been made harder by the decisions taken by successive governments.’
Post offices play a vital role in our communities
By Neil Brocklehurst, chief executive of the Post Office
During his first few weeks in office, Prime Minister Andy Burnham has made good growth in every postcode a defining objective of his Government. It’s a simple proposition. Economic success should not be confined to city centres or a handful of prosperous regions. It should be felt in our daily lives: on high streets and in villages across the UK.
Post Office chief executive Neil Brocklehurst
If we are serious about good growth in every postcode, we must be equally serious about what will make that possible.
Visit a post office on any morning and you’ll see what that looks like in practice. A small business owner depositing the previous day’s cash takings. Vinted and TikTok shop traders dropping off parcels. People of all ages depositing and withdrawing cash and paying their bills. These are ordinary moments, but together they are the building blocks of local economic activity and community life.
With 11,500 branches across the UK, a thriving Post Office network is not merely an accessory to growth in every postcode. It is a driving factor that makes growth possible.
Every week, more than ten million people and businesses visit a post office. The value of these visits goes further than just the money spent in branch: someone who drops off a parcel or pays a bill at the post office is likely to visit nearby businesses too. Collectively, this creates a halo effect worth £3billion of spend in nearby shops annually.
And then there’s the social impact of having a post office nearby. The public tells us there is a connection between community identity, pride and the state of the local high street. Over half say that a local post office fosters a sense of belonging to the community and is important to its identity.
Yet there is a contradiction at the heart of the Government’s ambition for growth. We say we want thriving high streets and essential services within easy reach of every community. But many of the businesses delivering exactly that are facing a sharp increase in costs.
Most post offices are independently run small businesses and they earn remuneration for each transaction carried out in branch. Now faced with rising costs, postmasters continue to tell me they are struggling. We are making urgent and essential changes to how Post Office operates to address this. Last year, we increased postmaster remuneration by over £86million – but it’s not enough against a backdrop of rising costs. For some, particularly in rural and isolated communities, these additional costs come at a time when margins are already under significant pressure.
Government has already accepted that pubs merit financial support because of their wider social and economic contribution to communities – with a 20 per cent cut to their business rates bill set to come into effect in England next year. Few would dispute the important role pubs play in bringing people together. But post offices play a similarly vital role in communities.
Recent changes to the business rates system mean post offices across the UK are forecast to pay almost £45million in business rates this year. That's around £29million more than branches paid under the previous relief system. Nearly 600 additional post offices will begin paying business rates for the first time, while the average bill is expected to rise to around £3,700. For rural post offices, the increase is particularly stark, with average rates bills expected to be around four times higher in 2026 than they were in 2023.
This burden is not just felt by the postmaster. If a branch closes, it is felt by the small business owner who relies on Post Office for banking services, or the vulnerable customer who prefers that face-to-face support, as well as nearby shops who see their footfall affected.
If the Government is serious about growth in every postcode, then it should recognise the unique role post offices play in making that growth possible.
That is why postmasters are calling for targeted business rates relief. This is not a request for special treatment. It is recognition that post offices are different from other retailers. They are community infrastructure: supporting other local businesses and providing services that many people would otherwise struggle to access.
The conversation about growth can often feel distant from people's daily lives. But growth in every postcode is not an abstract slogan. It is a small business able to keep trading, a busy high street, a village retaining vital services. Across Britain, postmasters are supporting good growth in every postcode every day, but they need urgent help in order to continue doing so.

items.title: Mini profile: Experienced retailer joins Spar with new store at Tutbury heritage site
items.summary: AF Blakemore has welcomed a new retailer into the Spar estate through its Blakemore Trade Partners plus offering with the opening of Spar Tutbury. This is an unusual site as it takes a standout conversion and brings one of the village’s most recognisable buildings back… This story continues at Mini profile: Experienced retailer joins Spar with new store at Tutbury heritage site Or just read more coverage at Talking Retail
items.body:
This is an unusual site as it takes a standout conversion and brings one of the village’s most recognisable buildings back into community use.
The store is owned by Kalpesh Odedra, an experienced retailer within a family-run business. Kalpesh purchased the site as a freehold and has undertaken a sensitive redevelopment of the former Lloyds Bank which closed in March 2022, and the Swinkles Family Brewers office that followed.
The building has been empty since 2024, and its Art Deco frontage, original front doors, safe door and vault have all been retained to create a store with genuine architectural character and a unique customer experience.
Spar Tutbury has been designed to serve basket-shopping missions, with a range tailored to local needs and a focus on fresh food, value and everyday essentials.
The store offers a premium wine and spirits range, dedicated Free From, Gluten Free and Vegan sections, and strong value through the County Bridge 3 for £9 fresh meat offer and Fresh Savers fruit and veg range.
A fresh Indian street food counter, including sweets, and a serve-over ice cream bar provide a distinctive food-to-go experience not previously available in the village.
The store will also offer a 12-week price promise on key essential lines through Price Lock until autumn.
Kalpesh Odedra said: “This building has always meant something to local people, and we wanted to bring it back into everyday use in a way that genuinely supports the community. “Spar’s focus on fresh food, everyday value and reliable service means we can offer Tutbury a store that feels welcoming, familiar and built around what shoppers need.
“Our aim is to create a place the village can be proud of and to keep this beautiful building alive for many years to come.
“We chose BTP+ [AF Blakemore’s retail support and reward program for independent Spar and convenience retailers in the UK] because it gives independent retailers the support, structure and confidence to deliver a stronger store for their community.
“The programme makes it easy to focus on fresh food, value and the right ranges, while still keeping the individuality of the site.
“For a building as unique as this one in Tutbury, BTP+ has helped us bring the space back to life in a way that feels modern, reliable and genuinely customer-focused.”
Taranjit Dhillon for AF Blakemore said: “This is an exceptional building and Kalpesh has done a remarkable job in bringing it back to life. Spar Tutbury is a perfect example of how heritage sites can be reimagined for modern convenience retailing, and we are delighted to support this development.”
Spar said the opening has created new employment opportunities and strengthens its presence in Staffordshire.

items.body:
Home improvement retailer Kingfisher taps AI tech driven personalisation as it ups profit target
Kingfisher Group, which owns B&Q and Screwfix in the UK and Castorama and Brico Depot in France and other markets, is using AI enabled productivity tools, including Fabric, to accelerate content creation, enhance SEO and improve conversion.
The FTSE 100 home improvement retailer lifted the lid on its AI and other tech initiatives as it raised its profit target despite seeing a heatwave driven drop off in sales at B&Q. It now expects to make a pre-tax profit of between £595 million and £635 million, having previously guided between £565 million and £625 million. Last year, it posted a £560 million profit.
Other highlights from its full year profit guidance and HY26/27 results include: group e-commerce sales reached 22% penetration. Group app sales now account for 29% of e-commerce sales, with app customers spending approximately 14% more than non-app users.
AI driven personalisation increased +16% generating approximately £100 million of sales, showing, Kingfisher claims, the growing value of its data and digital capabilities. Click & Collect sales were up +9% and home delivery sales +15%, supported by store-based fulfilment network and marketplace growth.
Screwfix Sprint (20 min delivery) was up +50% reflecting the growing demand for rapid fulfilment, particularly in Kingfisher’s City stores. Marketplace GMV rose +42% to £372 million, representing 18% of e-commerce sales. There has been investment in platform enhancements including Buybox, which helps customers find the best offer from multiple vendors by balancing price, merchant performance and delivery speed.
B&Q, meanwhile, continued to stump up cash for search and navigation capabilities, supporting improvements in online traffic and conversion. Natural language search is planned for implementation at B&Q in H2. The next phase of digital commerce will also include agent enabled shopping experiences.

In his welcome speech, Scott Thompson, Founder and Editor, RTIH, said: “This is the awards’ fifth year as a physical event. We started off with just 30 people at the South Place Hotel not far from here, then moved to London Bridge Hotel, then The Barbican, and last year RIBA’s HQ in the West End.”

items.title: Kingfisher shares rocket after B&Q owner lifts profit target
items.summary: Home improvement group Kingfisher saw its shares rocket after the group lifted its profit target, despite summer heatwaves pushing down sales at B&Q. The FTSE 100 retailer, which also owns Screwfix, said it now expects to make a pre-tax profit of between £595m and £635m, having previously guided between £565m and £625m. Last year, the [...]
items.body:
Kingfisher shares rocket after B&Q owner lifts profit target
Home improvement group Kingfisher saw its shares rocket after the group lifted its profit target, despite summer heatwaves pushing down sales at B&Q.
The FTSE 100 retailer, which also owns Screwfix, said it now expects to make a pre-tax profit of between £595m and £635m, having previously guided between £565m and £625m. Last year, the group posted a £560m profit.
Kingfisher’s shift towards “trade” customers – builders, plumbers and electricians – has driven this boost in forecasts, the group said. Its shares jumped by more than eight per cent to 332p in early trading.
The firm returned a pre-tax profit of £400m in the six months to July, improved by more than 18 per cent from last year. Like-for-like sales across the group edged up by 0.1 per cent.
But the group’s forecast was dragged down by the performance of B&Q, which suffered a 2.9 per cent drop-off in like-for-like sales, driven by a five per cent decline in the sale of “big ticket” items like kitchens and bathrooms.
Kingfisher said its bathroom ranges have “underperformed subdued markets,” adding that it has launched a “comprehensive” review into these products.
The group said sales fell at B&Q because record summer heatwaves drove customers away from shops and towards online shopping. The retailer’s market share remains “broadly stable,” it added.
Consumer environment ‘mixed’
B&Q recently launched its first trade-only store. Kingfisher said sales in this market remained “resilient,” gaining 0.2 per cent to £490m. The group has said it wants to reach £5bn in trade sales across its retailers.
Trade customers visit Kingfisher stores more often and spend more than retail customers, the group has found.
Sales at Screwfix jumped by 5.6 per cent in the six months to July, owing to a 7.3 per cent uplift in its seasonal ranges. The heatwaves boosted the sale of cooling products and garden seating, Kingfisher said.
The group saw a 2.2 per cent uplift in sales in its Polish market, while sales dipped by 2.3 per cent in France.
Kingfisher chief executive Thierry Garnier, who is set to leave the business, said the group’s shift towards trade customers and e-commerce is “creating new growth opportunities and strong financial discipline supporting performance across the business.
“While the consumer environment remains mixed, our consistent delivery, strategic progress and opportunities ahead give us the confidence to upgrade our guidance.”

items.body:
Former McDonald’s and Compass Group executive Jon Braithwaite connects with Co-op as new Group CDIO
Jon Braithwaite has joined Co-op as Interim Group Chief Digital and Information Officer. His CV includes stints at McDonald’s, Compass Group, and Gala Coral Group. Braithwaite is also an advisory board member at micro-donations specialist Pennies.
In a LinkedIn post, he said: “Co-op is a business that combines commercial scale with genuine social purpose, and few organisations are as trusted. Technology sits right at the heart of how we serve member-owners, customers and colleagues. I'm looking forward to working with the brilliant team here and building on the momentum already underway. Exciting times ahead.”
eStoreBrands
Digital commerce data specialist eStoreBrands has announced a new partnership with Co-op to launch Co-op Catalyst, an analytics platform for the quick commerce category. The platform gives suppliers direct access to Co-op's own q-commerce data across coop.co.uk and its delivery aggregator partners.
Suppliers can track product performance, search positioning and store level availability, and use the same data as their Co-op category team. Backed by Co-op's footprint of 2,300 convenience stores and its aggregator partnerships, Catalyst is pitched as providing an up-to-date view of the UK's quick commerce convenience market that has not been available to suppliers before.
Francis Nicholas, VP Product Strategy at eStoreBrands, says: "Having worked for brand owners including P&G and Nomad Foods, I know first-hand how valuable retailer insight is, and this is exactly what buying, category and quick commerce teams have been missing. Quick commerce is one of the fastest growing channels in digital retail, and Co-op Catalyst gives suppliers the retailer's own view of it, which site monitoring alone cannot provide. We look forward to helping suppliers make recommendations that benefit Co-op, their business and shoppers alike."
Kate McCrae, Operations and QCommerce Director, Co-op, says: "We're really excited about this partnership. Co-op is the UK's leading convenience store and a pioneer in Quick Commerce, where we now have around 90% reach across the UK. We are really excited about this new partnership and the insights and opportunities it will bring, as sharing deeper data will be instrumental in helping us, our suppliers, and partners serve Co-op members and shoppers. Co-op Catalyst will help unlock this channel, enabling suppliers to apply core Category Management principles to up-to-date data and recommend actions that accelerate growth for both their brands and Co-op."
Catalyst opens to suppliers later in 2026.

“But I’m conscious of the fact that, to quote the legend that is Taylor Swift, You’re only as hot as your last hit, baby. So, this year we’ve moved to our biggest venue yet, and also pulled in our largest number of entries to date and broken attendance records.”
He added: “This year’s submissions have without doubt been our best yet. To quote one of the judges: The examples of innovative developments across both traditional and digital retail spaces were truly remarkable.”
Congratulations to our winners, and a big thank you to our sponsors, judging panel, the legend that is Tiff Stevenson, and all those who attended our 2025 gathering.
Editor and Founder of Retail Technology Innovation Hub

items.body:
AI retail technology startup Thri5 builds on Wild Fork Foods pilot as it lands $5.4 million in seed funding
Thri5 has announced $5.4 million in seed funding following a pilot and roll-out with Wild Fork Foods. The round was co-led by Whitecap Venture Partners and Mistral Venture Partners, with participation from MaRS Investment Accelerator Fund (IAF), N49P and a group of retail and technology veterans.
Wild Fork has deployed Thri5’s AI technology across its store network in the United States and Canada.
“What I look for in any new tool is whether it connects what’s happening on the floor with what we plan centrally, and whether the team can actually trust the data. Thri5 does both. Adoption was fast because it told operators what mattered each day, not just what to look at,” says Radek Mazurkiewicz, COO at Wild Fork Foods.
Thri5 is built as an AI native execution layer that develops context across the enterprise, understanding what is happening across the business, how work gets done and where value is being lost. It continuously interprets signals across a retailer’s data and systems, identifies and prioritises the highest value opportunities, and connects head office priorities with field and store execution, orchestrating action across teams, systems and AI agents.
As work is completed, Thri5 learns from outcomes, building deeper operational context and improving how the organisation executes over time. Because it sits above retailers’ existing technology stack, it can coordinate execution across functions without requiring them to replace or migrate their core systems.
“Retailers don’t have a shortage of data, systems or plans. The challenge is translating all of that intelligence into the right action across every store. AI gives us a fundamentally different way to connect what the business knows with what teams actually do, continuously identifying where the biggest opportunities are, focusing teams on what matters most and learning from the results,” says Jeremy Pee, Co-Founder and CEO at Thri5.
Thri5 was founded by Pee and Herman Paek, COO. Pee most recently served as Chief Digital and Technology Officer of Marks & Spencer in the UK. Paek, meanwhile, was CEO and General Manager at Kijiji Canada. The two previously worked together to found and scale Loblaw Digital, building the digital business of Canada’s largest grocery and pharmacy retailer from the ground up into a multi-billion-dollar operation spanning online grocery, digital pharmacy and apparel.
“Jeremy and Herman have the combination we look for: deep domain expertise, proven operating experience and a history of building successfully together. They’ve experienced this problem firsthand and are now applying that experience to an enormous opportunity,” says Melissa Belbeck, Whitecap Venture Partners.
“AI’s biggest enterprise opportunity isn’t generating more insights - it’s turning intelligence into action. Thri5 is building the layer that makes that possible in retail. We believe the shift from systems of insight to systems of action represents an important new category of enterprise software,” says Raif Barbaros, Mistral Venture Partners.
With the new capital, Thri5 plans to expand its engineering, product and commercial teams and accelerate its go to market efforts with enterprise retailers globally.
